keep: Twelve screens alternate SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9) and DO (2, 4, 6, 8, 10), ending on two mixed puzzles (11 spring, 12 lifting machine), one example winding R = 0.04T + 10 carried through screens 1 to 6.
Example readings sit on a line that misses the origin, as the brief asks, and every number on the screens is an assumed reading or computed from rise ÷ run and y at x = 0.
The brief names one visible change (run and rise change together, the gradient in Ω per °C stays put) caused by one action (drag and stretch the triangle).

Sources are used on words their quotes support: [1] slope of V against I is the resistance, [2] volts per ampere, [4] gradient of force against extension is the spring constant, [5] and [9] the y = ax + b law with a and b defined, [7] the intercept, [12] the gradient from two points.

The DO screens carry the brief's mistakes with their own slips: gradient upside down (2, 11), one reading divided by its own temperature (2), first reading or x-axis crossing taken as c (4), the law used the wrong way round (6), higher read as steeper (8), axes swapped (10), b confused with the first reading or the gradient (12).
fix: Causal step skipped: the explanation never says why the stretched triangle gives the same gradient (a straight line climbs the same amount for each 1 along), why the crossing is R at 0 °C (at T = 0 the 0.04T part is 0, leaving c), or why the units divide (rise ÷ run divides ohms by degrees).

The PER 2016 trouble with lines that miss the origin is not shown failing: show one reading divided by its own temperature giving 10.8 ÷ 20 = 0.54 and 13.2 ÷ 80 = 0.165, different at each reading, because each reading includes the 10 Ω the winding had at 0 °C.

Slope/height confusion (Clement, 3 of 14) is on screens 7 and 8 but not taught in the explanation: add the two windings, A = 0.02T + 12 higher everywhere from 0 to 100 °C, B = 0.05T + 8 gaining 2.5 times as many ohms per degree.

Swapping the axes flips the gradient's unit, which the brief asks for and screens 9 and 10 use, is missing from the explanation: show 18 V ÷ 1.5 A = 12 Ω turning into 1.5 A ÷ 18 V, about 0.083 A per V, so read the axis labels first.

Faithfulness: 'the dependence on temperature' leaves out what depends; [3] is about how strongly a material resists current (resistivity), in many materials, so say that and keep 'many' and 'approximately'.
Honesty about the intercept: 0 °C lies below the readings, so 10 Ω is the line carried back, trusting it to stay straight there. Say so in explain and ignores, and draw that part dashed.
Text talks about the Ohm's law and spring cases instead of teaching them: give their worked numbers (12 Ω from 6 V at 0.5 A and 24 V at 2 A; 2.5 N per mm from 10 N at 4 mm and 30 N at 12 mm).

Analogy reproduces only the shape, not the units: say the standing charge is in pounds and the unit rate in pounds per kWh, so the gradient's unit is y's unit per x's unit, and make 'breaks' specific (a tariff is set first and can have more than one rate).

Practice mistakes are named, not shown failing with numbers, and miss the one-reading shortcut, swapped axes and reading c where a drawn axis starts above 0 (taught as a check, since no source counts it).
whatAmILookingAt does not say what b means on screen 12 (the effort with no load on, read from the graph, with no claim about its cause) or that the carried-back part of the line is dashed.
